title: Replication Models & Quorums
body:
# Replication Models & Quorums

<BurgerAnalogy text={"Our burger restaurant keeps three copies of the digital order ledger and can require acknowledgments from two before confirming a write. Reading two copies ensures overlap with that write's acknowledgment set under the same replica membership. The overlap is useful, but version selection, concurrent writes, and failure handling still matter; counting responses alone does not establish every strong-consistency guarantee."} />

Replication keeps copies of data on multiple nodes for **durability**, **availability**, and **read scaling**. The hard part is keeping those copies consistent. There are three broad models and one unifying idea: the **quorum**.

## The three models

<Cards cols={3}>

<Card title="Leader–Follower" accent="brand">

One leader takes writes and streams them to followers. This simplifies write ordering, but follower reads may be stale unless the protocol and read settings provide stronger guarantees. The leader can become a write bottleneck and needs a failover strategy.

</Card>

<Card title="Multi-Leader" accent="purple">

Several leaders accept writes (often one per region). Great for write locality, but **write conflicts** must be resolved.

</Card>

<Card title="Leaderless" accent="green">

Any replica accepts reads and writes (Dynamo, Cassandra). Clients use **quorums** to stay consistent.

</Card>

</Cards>

## Quorums: the R + W > N rule

In a leaderless system with **N** replicas, a write must be acknowledged by **W** of them and a read must consult **R** of them. The key inequality:

<Callout type="info" title="The overlap guarantee">

If **R + W > N**, a read set and a successfully acknowledged write set drawn from the **same N replicas** must **overlap** in at least one node. Without intervening writes, the read can contact a replica containing that acknowledged version. This is a set-overlap property, not a complete proof of strong consistency or linearizability.

The protocol must also select versions correctly and handle concurrent or incomplete writes, replica membership changes, and repair. A sloppy quorum that temporarily uses other replicas may not preserve the assumed overlap. Linearizable operations need additional protocol guarantees; for example, Cassandra uses Paxos-backed lightweight transactions for that purpose, rather than obtaining them from the quorum inequality alone.

</Callout>

- **W = N, R = 1** — fast reads, slow/fragile writes
- **W = 1, R = N** — fast writes, slow reads
- **W = R = ⌈(N+1)/2⌉** — balanced majority quorum

Lowering R and W below the overlap threshold trades consistency for **availability and latency** — reads may return stale values until anti-entropy (read repair, hinted handoff) catches up.

<Callout type="success" title="Try it">

Tune N, W, and R, issue writes and reads, and watch stale reads appear when the quorums stop overlapping in the [Quorum Replication Simulator](/dados-armazenamento/replication-quorums/simulator).

</Callout>

## Related ideas

This connects directly to the [CAP theorem](/theoretical-foundations/cap-theorem): a partition can make the required quorum unreachable, forcing an operation to wait or fail. Reducing the required responses can improve availability but weakens the assumptions behind version freshness; it is not a universal linear consistency/availability slider. See [Apache Cassandra consistency guarantees](https://cassandra.apache.org/doc/latest/cassandra/architecture/guarantees.html).
